claims.text: Optimized friction stir processing can repair or improve damaged HSLA-steel or 17-4PH stainless-steel surfaces.
FSP will produce a significantly refined, equiaxed microstructure in these steels.
FSP will induce compressive residual stresses in the processed surface.
The refined microstructure and compressive residual stresses will minimize hot cracking.
FSP will enhance surface hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to fusion-welded repairs and untreated surfaces.
Damaged HSLA-steel or 17-4PH stainless-steel components previously subjected to fusion-welding repair have coarse, heterogeneous microstructures and segregation issues.
Moderate FSP tool rotational speeds for the proposed treatment are 500–1000 rpm.
Controlled traverse rates and temperature monitoring can provide uniform plastic deformation during FSP.
The proposed FSP treatment can be conducted under ambient atmosphere while remaining below the steel melting point.
Real-time parameter monitoring can prevent localized overheating and ensure homogeneous dynamic recrystallization.
Intense localized plastic deformation during FSP causes dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement.
FSP reduces chemical segregation and inherent stress concentrations.
Fine grains and compressive residual stresses mitigate crack initiation and propagation.
Reducing crack-initiation sites will extend service life in aggressive environments.
Traditional fusion-weld repairs produce coarse, heterogeneous microstructures with tensile or neutral residual stresses.
The benefits of FSP are confined to the processed surface layer.
Service temperatures high enough to alter the refined microstructure may eliminate the expected benefits.
The magnitude of improvement depends on process parameters, material composition, and initial damage extent.
Real-time monitoring should reduce variability in the FSP result.
